summary: Oversized, unmanaged buffers in networks cause a range of performance problems, and Active Queue Management (AQM) schemes, sometimes combined with packet scheduling, can help. This informational document describes criteria and guidelines for characterizing and comparing AQM mechanisms, so that evaluations are done in a consistent way.

eli5.summary: If too many people line up at one doorway, the line gets huge and slow. Queue managers decide who waits and who is turned away early. This explains how to test whether a queue manager does its job well.

questions: how do you test an aqm algorithm
what is bufferbloat and how does aqm help
how should you measure latency and throughput for aqm
what makes a fair aqm comparison
subtitle: Guidelines for testing and evaluating queue management algorithms

tldr.problem: Networks have large unmanaged buffers that cause high latency and poor performance (bufferbloat). Active Queue Management (AQM) algorithms can help, but there was no standard way to test and compare them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7928 provides characterization guidelines: a set of standard scenarios, metrics, and evaluation procedures that testers can use to assess whether an AQM algorithm reduces latency and maintains throughput without breaking network behavior.
tldr.outcome: Implementers and researchers can now fairly evaluate AQM algorithms against consistent criteria, comparing them with each other and against traditional drop-tail queuing to determine safety and performance benefits.

today: RFC 7928 is an Informational RFC published in July 2016 and represents the consensus of the IETF community. It remains the standard reference for evaluating Active Queue Management algorithms and has guided the testing and standardization of new AQM mechanisms like CoDel and PIE.

sections.title: The Bufferbloat Problem
sections.content:
Modern networks suffer from a problem called bufferbloat. Routers and switches have very large buffers (often 10 to 100 times larger than needed) to improve throughput, but they do not actively manage the queues. When congestion occurs, packets can sit in these enormous buffers for hundreds of milliseconds, causing high latency. This especially hurts interactive applications like video calls, gaming, and web browsing, where users expect quick response times.

Active Queue Management (AQM) algorithms address this by actively dropping or marking packets when the queue starts to grow, signaling to senders to slow down before the buffer overflows. Classical algorithms like RED have existed for decades, but more recent ones like CoDel and PIE show promise. However, without a standard way to evaluate these algorithms, it is hard to know which ones actually work, and whether they are safe to deploy without breaking network behavior.
sections.eli5: Big buffers in routers make the network slow because packets sit waiting. Queue managers can drop packets early to tell senders to slow down, but people need a fair way to test whether a queue manager actually helps.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Metrics
sections.content:
RFC 7928 defines a set of end-to-end metrics for evaluating AQM. Latency is the one-way delay of packets, and minimizing it is the goal of AQM. Goodput is the application-layer throughput (bits per second delivered to the destination), minus any losses or retransmissions. Jitter is the variation in packet delay. Packet loss and loss synchronization (whether all flows lose packets at the same time) are also important. An AQM must reduce latency while keeping goodput high and avoiding synchronized losses that hurt fairness.

The document also distinguishes between queue-length-based algorithms (like RED, which look at how many packets are queued) and queuing-delay-based algorithms (like CoDel and PIE, which measure actual delay). These different approaches may have different control parameters and behaviors, so testers must be careful when comparing them.
sections.eli5: Tests should measure how fast packets arrive, how much good data gets through, whether the queue looks even, and whether packets from all senders lose data at the same time.

sections.title: Generic Testing Setup
sections.content:
RFC 7928 recommends a simple network topology for testing: multiple senders on one side connected through a bottleneck router with AQM to multiple receivers on the other side. The bottleneck link is the scarce resource where queues form. Testers should measure both symmetric scenarios (same capacity in both directions) and asymmetric ones (more capacity one way, like real broadband links).

The buffer size should typically equal the bandwidth-delay product (capacity times the largest round-trip time in the network). Testers should evaluate the AQM with different congestion control algorithms: TCP NewReno (standard), CUBIC (aggressive), and LEDBAT (less-than-best-effort). The same tests should be run multiple times to gather statistical confidence in the results. Setup details and software versions must be documented so others can replicate the tests.
sections.eli5: Build a simple test network with senders on one side, a queue manager in the middle, and receivers on the other side. Run the same test many times and write down all the details.

sections.title: Key Evaluation Scenarios
sections.content:
RFC 7928 outlines several critical scenarios. RTT (Round-Trip Time) Fairness tests whether flows with long delays (slow links) get a fair share of bandwidth compared to flows with short delays. Burst Absorption tests whether the AQM can handle sudden traffic spikes without excessive packet loss. Stability tests how the algorithm behaves under varying congestion levels (mild, medium, and heavy) and whether it oscillates or converges smoothly.

Tests should also vary traffic profiles (mixtures of TCP, aggressive, and unresponsive flows), include bidirectional traffic, evaluate parameter sensitivity (how much the algorithm's performance changes if you tweak its knobs), and test multiple AQM instances interacting on the same network. The goal is to find scenarios where an AQM fails or where its benefits disappear, not just the best-case results.
sections.eli5: Test slow flows against fast ones, sudden traffic bursts, stable and changing congestion, different types of traffic, and see what breaks the queue manager.

sections.title: Fair Comparison
sections.content:
When comparing two AQM algorithms, testers must be careful about parameters. Different algorithms expose different control knobs with different meanings. For example, RED uses a target queue length (in bytes or packets), while CoDel uses a target queuing delay (in milliseconds). Setting RED to 100 MB and CoDel to 10 ms are very different operating points. Fair comparison requires either (1) understanding what each parameter does and setting them for equivalent behavior, or (2) comparing over a range of parameter settings for each algorithm.

Comparison should also separate performance considerations (latency, goodput, fairness) from deployment considerations (implementation cost, parameter sensitivity, whether it auto-tunes, whether it works in routers). An AQM that is slightly slower should not be rejected if it is much simpler to deploy or more robust.
sections.eli5: Different queue managers have different dials to turn. You have to turn them fairly or test both at many different settings to compare fairly.

sections.title: From Testing to Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 7928 emphasizes that characterization guidelines do not mandate a particular toolset or require all AQM proposals to follow them for standardization. Instead, the guidelines help testers understand what an AQM should be tested against, particularly in their own deployment context. A home network, a data center, or a wireless WLAN may benefit from different AQM algorithms, and testers should tailor scenarios to their environment.

The document also recommends discussing operator control (whether and how network administrators can tune the AQM) and auto-tuning (whether the algorithm can adapt its parameters automatically based on network conditions). These considerations matter for real-world deployment. Finally, testers are encouraged to publish detailed test setups and results so others can compare and build on their work.
sections.eli5: Use these guidelines in the network setting you care about, talk about whether the queue manager can be tuned, and share your test results so others can compare.
